description.value: The study examined whether simple multiplication processing differs between the language in which bilingual adults learned multiplication and their other language, using behavioral measures and fMRI-defined language and quantity regions.

design.value: Thirty-five Spanish-English bilingual adults completed verbal and numerosity localizer tasks and a single-digit multiplication verification task during one experimental session. The verbal and multiplication tasks were administered in English and Spanish, with language order alternated across participants. The final analyzed sample comprised 29 participants.

description.value: Test 14 of the Woodcock-Johnson Tests of Achievement, used to assess vocabulary in English.
The parallel Spanish Picture Vocabulary subtest from the Batería III Woodcock-Muñoz, used to assess vocabulary in Spanish.
Test 15 of the Woodcock-Johnson Tests of Achievement and its parallel Spanish version from the Batería III Woodcock-Muñoz, used to assess language comprehension.
Test 8 of the Woodcock-Johnson Tests of Cognitive Abilities and its parallel Spanish version from the Batería III Woodcock-Muñoz, used to assess phonological awareness.
A Wechsler Individual Achievement Test subtest in which participants answered as many single-digit multiplication problems as possible in 60 seconds.
The Edinburgh Inventory was used to assess handedness; participants' scores ranged from 0.35 to 1.00.

source_definition.value: Language of learning multiplication (LA+) versus the other language (LA-).
Problems with correct solutions smaller than 25 were considered small problems, and problems with correct solutions larger than 25 were considered large problems.
The correctness of the proposed solution: true or false.
A language (LA+, LA-) by problem size (small, large) interaction.

Vocabulary fluency in the other language, measured using the Picture Vocabulary subtest of the Woodcock-Johnson Tests of Achievement and the parallel Vocabulario Sobre Dibujos subtest of the Batería III.
Vocabulary fluency in the language of learning multiplication, entered into the hierarchical regression models as a covariate of no interest.
Subjects were included as a random effect in the linear mixed models.
Six motion parameters estimated during realignment were entered in the first-level modeling as regressors.

description.value: The final sample comprised 29 Spanish-English bilingual adults. All participants reported Spanish as their native language, 8 also reported English as a simultaneous native language, 11 learned multiplication in Spanish, and 18 learned multiplication in English.

excluded_count.value: Six of the initial 35 participants were excluded from the final sample.

recruitment_method.value: Thirty-five Spanish-English bilingual adults were recruited, with 5 from the University of Texas at Austin and 30 from the University of Houston.

medical_condition.value: no history of cognitive or perceptual deficits; no diagnosed language delays or learning disabilities

medication_status.value: Participants were not taking medication that affected their cognition at the time of testing; one participant was excluded for taking psychoactive medications at the time of testing.

task_description.value: Participants heard two spoken number words, followed by a visual Arabic digit, and determined whether the Arabic digit was the correct product of the two spoken numbers. Two runs were presented in English and two runs in Spanish.

instructions.value: Participants were instructed to determine whether the Arabic digit was the correct product of the two spoken numbers. They used their index finger if the proposed solution was true and their middle finger if the proposed solution was false.

stimuli.value: Two spoken single-digit number words followed by a visual Arabic digit. Participants did not see any written words. Proposed solutions were presented as an Arabic digit in both languages.

task_description.value: Participants saw a black-and-white line drawing of an object followed by a spoken word and determined whether the word matched the presented picture or not. They completed two runs in English and two runs in Spanish.

instructions.value: Participants determined whether the spoken word matched the presented picture or not. They used their index finger if the picture-word pairs matched and their middle finger if they did not match.

stimuli.value: A black-and-white line drawing of an object followed by a spoken word in English or Spanish.

task_description.value: Participants determined which of two sequentially presented dot arrays contained more dots. They completed two runs.

instructions.value: Participants were tasked with determining which of two sequentially presented dot arrays contained more dots.

stimuli.value: Sequentially presented dot arrays with easy comparisons at a ratio of 1:3, medium comparisons at a ratio of 1:2, and hard comparisons at a ratio of 2:3. Dot size was controlled across arrays.

modality.value: fMRI blood oxygenation level dependent (BOLD) signal

instrument.value: Siemens Prisma Fit scanner (3T) at the Baylor College of Medicine’s Core for Advanced Magnetic Resonance Imaging (Houston, Texas)

description.value: The BOLD signal was measured with a susceptibility-weighted single-shot echo planar imaging (EPI) sequence. Parameters were TE = 30 ms, flip angle = 68 s, matrix size = 256 x 256, field of view = 256, slice thickness = 2 mm, number of slices = 64, TR = 1,250 ms, and voxel size = 2 x 2 x 2 mm.

modality.value: fMRI blood oxygenation level dependent (BOLD) signal

instrument.value: Siemens Skyra scanner (3T) at the University of Texas’s Biomedical Imaging Center (Austin, Texas)

description.value: The BOLD signal was measured with a susceptibility-weighted single-shot echo planar imaging (EPI) sequence. Parameters were TE = 30 ms, flip angle = 68 s, matrix size = 256 x 256, field of view = 256, slice thickness = 2 mm, number of slices = 64, TR = 1,250 ms, and voxel size = 2 x 2 x 2 mm.

instrument.value: Siemens Prisma Fit scanner and Siemens Skyra scanner, both 3T

description.value: Before functional image acquisition, a high-resolution T1-weighted 3D structural image was acquired for each participant with TR = 1,900 ms, TE = 2.43 ms, matrix size = 256 x 256, field of view = 256 mm, slice thickness = 1 mm, and number of slices = 192.

Preprocessing and analysis of the fMRI data was computed using Statistical Parametric Mapping (SPM12). Functional images were realigned, co-registered to a skull-stripped anatomical image, normalized to the standard T1 Montreal Neurological Institute template, smoothed, and corrected for movement-related outlier volumes using Art-Repair.

steps.value: All functional images were realigned to their mean functional image across runs.
An anatomical brain mask was created by combining the segmentation products of grey matter, white matter, and cerebrospinal fluid.
The anatomical brain mask was applied to the original anatomical image to produce a skull-stripped anatomical image.
The mean functional image and all functional images were co-registered to the skull-stripped anatomical image.
All functional images were normalized to the standard T1 Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI) template.
Smoothing was applied to all functional images with a 6 mm isotropic Gaussian kernel.
Art-Repair was used to identify outlier volumes, defined by excessive head movement or deviations of more than 4% from the mean global signal intensity.
Outlier volumes were repaired by interpolation between the nearest non-outlier volumes.
Six motion parameters estimated during realignment were entered in the first-level modeling as regressors, and repaired volumes were deweighted.

model_settings.value: Activation was modeled as epochs time-locked to the first stimulus in each trial. All proposed solutions and all participants' responses were included. The time series was high-pass filtered at 1/128 Hz, serial correlations were corrected using an autoregressive AR model, six realignment motion parameters were included as regressors, and repaired volumes were deweighted.
Models included Language, Problem size, and Correctness, with Subjects as a random effect. Satterthwaite's method was used to estimate denominator degrees of freedom for F statistics.

software.value: generalized linear model from the lme4 package in R

model_settings.value: LA+ vocabulary fluency was entered as a covariate of no interest and LA- vocabulary fluency as the independent variable. The dependent measure was the difference in multiplication-task performance or brain activation across languages.

Brain data were modeled based on Problem Size, Language, and the additive effect with and without the interaction between the two. WAIC was used to compare models, and posterior summaries provided Bayesian p-values. A 95% highest posterior density interval not containing 0 was considered significant.

estimator.value: Watanabe information criteria comparison and posterior summaries

model_type.value: cluster-wise thresholding using Monte Carlo simulations

model_settings.value: Ten thousand Monte Carlo simulations were conducted using a cluster-wise probability threshold of 0.05 and a voxel-wise threshold of 0.005 within each ROI. Cluster size thresholds were calculated using participant-averaged smoothness values from 3dFWHMx.
